newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: INSTANT VIEW - Market takes NZ GDP data in stride.
newsitem.headline: INSTANT VIEW - Market takes NZ GDP data in stride.

text.p: Following are economists' reactions to New Zealand September quarter GDP data published on Thursday.

Seasonally-adjusted production-based Gross Domestic Product rose 0.6 percent for the quarter and the annual average rate was 2.3 percent, versus economists' forecasts of 0.2 percent and 2.25 percent respectively.

Thirty minutes after the data were released, the New Zealand dollar was trading at US$0.7031/38 versus 0.7039/46 shortly beforehand, while 90-day bank bill rates were at 7.35 percent versus 7.32 percent.
BANKERS TRUST CHIEF ECONOMIST DAVID PLANK
"I'm surprised that the past has not been revised up. I was expecting to see upward revisions of previous growth, but they've actually revised the year to March down slightly."
"I think the policy implications of this are very minor."
Plank noted that manufactured exports were up, despite the strength of the New Zealand dollar.
STEPHEN TOPLIS, DOYLE PATERSON BROWN ECONOMIST
"The bottomline number is stronger than expected but if you go through and look at why it is as strong as it is, then I don't think there is anything in there to shock anyone.

"If you take out that big lumpy investment which most people knew about but never fully built into their numbers, it gets rid of a point or two. I suspect people underestimated just how much was coming out of the dairy sector. If you look underneath that and say 'Structurally how strong is the economy?', manufacturing excluding dairy was very flat, retailing was flat to negative. Look at investment minus an oil tanker and it is negative. It is
a very flat economy."
Statistics NZ said the rise in business investment for the quarter was mainly the result of the one-off import of an oil tanker for use at the Maui-B rig.
Toplis said the figures were historical and would not have any impact on the government's accounts.

"It's ancient history. Someone might get excited short-term and see a bigger number and decide it's a reason they can't loosen monetary policy for another week. Overall I would be very surprised if it changed anyone's views."
Marshall said he expected December quarter growth to be well down and for that quarter to be the turning point in the cycle.
He said the September quarter figure did not change his outlook. "December quarter will be flat and the March and June quarters will be fairly flat as well."
BANCORP ECONOMIST STUART MARSHALL
Marshall said little inference could be drawn from the outcome given the historical nature of the series.

"Imports looks an interesting result to rise only 0.9 percent. That will be one to look at a bit deeper to see what the volume was. It was such a small rise when the exchange rate rose by 4.7 percent in the quarter," he said.
JASON WONG, ECONOMIST, FIRST NZ CAPITAL
"It was a little bit higher than expected but a lot of the growth went into stock building so it's not necessarily a sign of strength.
"If consumption and domestic demand don't pick up, then all of a sudden you are left with all this stock which implies weakness further down the track.
"I still think there is some weakness there, especially in the primary and productive areas like manufacturing. What's holding our numbers up is a very strong services sector.
"That trend has been continuing for a year now and we are still a few months away from a pick-up."
Asked how the Reserve Bank would view the numbers, he said: "I don't think it has any significant implications for monetary policy."
He said the September quarter data was historical and the market was likely to focus on the more recent sectoral indicators for an indication of the economy's performance.
"I think the 'mixed' word is going to come into the vocabulary. It is pretty patchy."
He said some retailers had a good Christmas and others said it was poor, so overall it was likely to have been flat.
ADRIAN ORR, CHIEF ECONOMIST, NATIONAL BANK
"It certainly helps explain a little bit why inflation's been so persistent.

"Going through the components, it's nothing that should upset the Reserve Bank...Gross national expenditure, in other words domestic expenditure, is only 0.3 for the quarter and most of that's made up of investment, with private consumption and government consumption down. So as far as inflation-reducing stuff goes, it's about as good as you can get, and exports running ahead of imports, so that's pretty good from the RB's perspective." -- Wellington newsroom 64 4 473-4746
